modules.html:
What does SER express?

SER expresses something or someone's essence. Any quality or attribute that defines how that essence is perceived by someone can be expressed with SER.
⚠️Careful with the word "permanent" when talking about SER

Many teachers, materials, or even influencers might tell you that SER is used for "permanent" traits. Seems simple, right? At first it seems to hold up. Most characteristcs that are more "permanent" can be attributed just fine with SER, but it can also cause confusion.

Let’s take this sentence:

Guadalajara está en Jalisco, México.
Guadalajara is in Jalisco, Mexico.

Wait—location seems pretty permanent. Cities don’t teleport. So why use ESTAR instead of SER?

Because location is not part of what a city is, conceptually speaking—it's part of where it is. That’s a situational context, not an identity trait. We're not describing what Guadalajara is like—we're situating it! More on this later on!

Let's take another sentence:

Era bastante tímido cuando era niño.
I was pretty shy when I was a kid.

Well, I was shy but I'm not anymore, so why can't I just say "estaba tímido"?

Because we're describing how someone was perceived, how they were as a person at that time. It’s about identity, not a fleeting emotion or reaction. Even if it changed later, it was their essence then.

There's nothing that says essence is fixed forever—it can evolve. As Eduardo Galeano put it:

Somos lo que hacemos para cambiar lo que somos.
We are what we do to change what we are.

Explore Examples of Common Attributes that Mark Essence

Identity
Juan y Carla son mis mejores amigos.
Juan and Carla are my best friends.

Esta película es mi favorita.
This movie is my favorite.

Origin

Mi abuela es de México.
My grandmother is from Mexico.

Estos vinos son de Argentina.
These wines are from Argentina.

Brand
Mi celular es un iPhone.
My cell is an iPhone.

Esos zapatos son Nike.
Those shoes are Nike.

Personality

Mi hermana es muy extrovertida.
My sister is very outgoing.

Marcos es una persona muy paciente.
Marcos is a very patient person.

Material

Esta mesa es de madera.
This table is made of wood.

Mis anillos son de plata.
My rings are made of silver.

Color

Mi coche es rojo.
My car is red.

Estas paredes son blancas.
These walls are white.

Qualities

El café es amargo sin azúcar.
Coffee is bitter without sugar.

Su voz es muy suave.
Her/His voice is very soft.

Profession

Mi papá es médico.
My dad is a doctor.

Ellos son profesores de historia.
They are history teachers.

Personal Relationships

Carolina es mi prima.
Carolina is my cousin.

Nosotros somos novios.
We're a couple (boyfriend & girlfriend/boyfriends)

Category

Los gatos son mamíferos.
Cats are mammals.

Este libro es una novela de ciencia ficción.
This book is a science fiction novel.

Shape

La mesa es redonda.
The table is round.

Mis gafas son rectangulares.
My glasses are rectangular.

Dates

Hoy es martes.
Today is Tuesday.

Mi cumpleaños es el 10 de abril.
My birthday is on April 10th.

Times

Ahora es la una y media de la tarde.
Right now, it is 1:30 in the afternoon.

Son las 17 horas. / Son las cinco de la tarde.
It’s 5:00 pm.

La reunión es a las cinco.
The meeting is at five.


What does ESTAR express?

ESTAR expresses someone or something’s situation. This can include any temporary state, condition, or location that is experienced, perceived, or subject to change. It reflects how that person or thing is situated in a specific moment or context—physically, emotionally, or circumstantially—rather than what defines their essence.
Explore Examples of Common Situations that Mark ESTAR

Location (Physical Presence)

Mi mochila está en el auto.
My backpack is in the car.

Ellos están en la sala de reuniones.
They are in the meeting room.

Emotional State

Hoy estoy muy contenta.
Today I'm very happy.

Mi hermano está un poco triste.
My brother is a little sad.

Physical Condition

El café está caliente.
The coffee is hot.

La computadora está apagada.
The computer is off.

Health

Estoy muy agotada.
I’m exhausted.

Mi abuela está enferma.
My grandmother is sick.

Ongoing Actions (Progressive Aspect)

Estoy estudiando para el examen.
I am studying for the exam.

Ellos están trabajando en el proyecto.
They are working on the project.

Weather / Environmental Conditions

Está un poco nublado hoy.
It’s a bit cloudy today.

¿Cómo está el clima allá?
How’s the weather over there?

Marital / Relationship Status

Mis padres están casados.
My parents are married.

Estoy divorciado.
I'm divorced.

*SER can be used with casado, divorciado, and soltero when describing civil status as a social category or identity (essence). We'll cover this more in depth later on when we look at SER and ESTAR with adjectives.

Appearances Traits Marking a Sudden Change

Marta está muy guapa hoy.
Marta looks very pretty today.

Ese actor está más delgado últimamente.
That actor looks thinner lately.

Situational Reactions

¡Esta torta está riquísima!
This cake is delicious!

Tu presentación estuvo excelente.
Your presentation was excellent.

Availability / Presence

Lo siento, el director no está ahora.
Sorry, the director isn't here right now.

Podés sentarte acá, está libre la silla.
You can sit here, the chair’s free.

Dead or Alive

Mi abuelo ya no está.
My grandfather is no longer with us.

¿Está viva la planta?
Is the plant alive?

Below is a brief overview of the core concepts of SER and ESTAR. As you study the examples, notice how SER consistently marks essence, while ESTAR consistently marks situation.

modules.title: The Basics of SER & ESTAR

modules.html:
Overview


ESTAR expresses a location when we locate situations, material entities, or mental presences—things that “are somewhere” as part of their current state or circumstance.

This distinction follows the central operational principle:

  • SER = essence, identity, inherent definition. An event's location is an essential characteristic of its existense. Events can only exist in time and space, so both their location and time can only be considered an essential characteristic.
  • ESTAR = situation, circumstance, placement in space or mental presence.  ESTAR places something in a physical or mental space as part of its current situation.
    If you can imagine pointing at it, visiting it, being next to it, or “finding” it, Spanish instinctively uses ESTAR because we think about its location situationally.
SER expresses a location when that location is understood as an essential property of an event or destination. 

ESTAR + Location 

Material Entities

People, animals, objects, and places are located with ESTAR because their position is part of their situational reality, not their identity.

Los jugadores están en la cancha.
The players are on the field.

El auto está en el taller.
The car is in the shop.

¿Quiénes estuvieron en la fiesta?
Who was at the party?

This also includes geographical locations. We treat the location of cities, countries, and other geographic regions as a situational reality in relation to the location of other material entities.

Mendoza está en Argentina.
Mendoza is in Argentina.

Portland está en Oregon.
Portland is in Oregon.

You may be tempted to use SER to express where a city is if you think of it's location as being a permanent feature, but remember, permanence has nothing to do with SER.

Mental or Conceptual Presences

Spanish often “materializes” abstract ideas so they can “be somewhere.” That's why we use ESTAR even when we talk about the location of concepts that don't seem all that material such as love or thoughts.
El amor está en todas partes.
Love is everywhere.

Mis pensamientos están con vos.
My thoughts are with you.

Here ESTAR anchors intangible concepts into a felt or imagined space.

SER + Location

Events and Actions

SER is used when we talk about where events and actions happen. The location of an event is part of its essence.

If the sentence answers the question “Where is the event happening as an essential characteristic of it?”, Spanish chooses SER.

Events (parties, classes, games, meetings, accidents) do not “exist in space” the way people or objects do. You cannot “find a party sitting somewhere.” Instead, an event's location is a conceptual identity, defined (in part) by where it takes place.
El partido es en el nuevo estadio.
The game is in the new stadium.

¿Dónde fue el accidente?
Where was the accident?

La fiesta va a ser en mi casa.
The party is going to be at my house.

La clase es en Google Meet.
The class is (held) on Google Meet.

¿En qué canal es el programa?
What channel is the program on?

Why SER here? Because “game,” “class,” “accident,” “program,” etc. are events whose identity includes where they are held or broadcast. The location is not a circumstance—it's a defining feature.

Destination

When SER answers “Is this the place?”, we are identifying a destination point, almost like labeling a spot on a map.
  • —¡Es acá! —le dije al taxista.
    "It's here!" I said to the cab driver.
  • —No, aquí no es. Es más adelante.
    “No, it’s not here. It’s further ahead.”

We use SER because we’re not locating an object—we’re identifying a target point, the essential destination of a journey.

Summary

ESTAR = “to be situated / to be findable.”

  • Used for: people, objects, animals, places, mental or conceptual presences.
  • Meaning: location describes current state or placement.
  • Key question: Are we locating a thing in space? → ESTAR

    SER = “to take place / to be defined as happening somewhere.”

    • Used for: people, objects, animals, places, mental or conceptual presences.
    • Meaning: location is an essential characteristic of the event.
    • Key question: Are we locating where an event takes place or identifying a destination? → SER

In Spanish, we often use SER or ESTAR with a participle (like firmado, construida, escrito)—but why? It's about how we understand what something is vs. how something is.

SER + participle: What defines it (action as identity)

We use SER + participle when we describe an action as part of what something is—its identity, origin, purpose, or how it came to be. These actions are not just things that happened—they're part of how we define or classify the thing.

Think of it as answering the question:
What happened to this as part of what it is?

Examples of essential attributes of actions:

El documento fue firmado por el director.
The document was signed by the director. 

La ciudad fue construida en el siglo XIX.
The city was constructed in the 19th century.

Ese libro fue escrito por un famoso historiador.
That book was written by a famous historian.

Las leyes fueron aprobadas por el Congreso.
The laws were approved by Congress.

El proyecto fue diseñado para ayudar a los estudiantes.
The project was designed to help students.

ESTAR + participle: What condition it's in (action as result)

We use ESTAR + participle when we describe a current condition or state—a situation that results from an action. It's not about identity; it’s about how the thing is now.

Think of it as answering the question:
How is this now, after something happened to it?

Examples of resulting states of actions:

El documento está firmado.
The document is signed.

La ciudad está construida.
The city is built. 

El libro está traducido al español.
The book is translated into Spanish. 

Las leyes ya están aprobadas.
The lawys are now passed.

El proyecto está finalizado.
The project is finalized.



Summary

  • SER + participle expresses an action that is essential to the identity of the subject. It tells us what happened to create it.
  • ESTAR + participle expresses the resulting state of an action.

¡A practicar!

modules.html:
SER and ESTAR with Adjectives: A Conceptual Perspective

Choosing between SER and ESTAR with adjectives is not just a matter of grammar—it's a matter of perspective. Each verb invites the speaker and listener to frame the situation in a different way. SER typically presents the adjective as part of how something or someone is characterized within a broader, more stable frame of reference—often linked to identity, classification, or general evaluation. In contrast, ESTAR presents the adjective as part of a more focused, immediate frame—often highlighting how something is experienced, perceived, or assessed in a specific context or situation.

This section is designed to help you notice how the verb you choose shifts the meaning of the adjective, sometimes subtly, sometimes dramatically. The slides will guide you through real examples that illustrate these contrasts. Once you’ve reviewed them, try the interactive activities to apply what you’ve learned and solidify your understanding. 

SER & ESTAR With Relationship Status (soltero, casado, divorciado)

In everyday Spanish, you might hear both ser and estar used to talk about marital status — for example: estar casado vs. ser casado. But they don’t mean quite the same thing. So what's the difference?

Use ESTAR to describe a current state or situation.

When a speaker uses estar with words like soltero, casado, or divorciado, they’re treating marital status as something situational or changeable — often in contrast to what came before or what might come next. It’s about how someone is in a given context, not who they are in essence.

Estaba de novio durante unos meses, pero no funcionó y ahora estoy soltero desde diciembre.
I was dating someone for a few months, but it didn’t work out and now I’ve been single since December.

Mi hermano está comprometido con su novia desde hace meses.
My brother has been engaged to his girlfriend for several months.

Juan y María están divorciados, pero siguen siendo buenos amigos
Juan and María are divorced, but they’re still good friends.

Juan y María estuvieron casados diez años
Juan and María were married for ten years.

In these cases, estar points to a current or past state, often one that could change again.

Use SER to describe marital status as a category or identity.

With ser, the focus shifts. Now we’re not describing someone’s state or situation — we’re classifying them. Think of ser here as assigning a social identity or status (like soltero, casado, divorciado) that defines what kind of person someone is, or which category they belong to.

Juan es divorciado.
Juan is a divorced man.

Roberta es casada.
Roberta is a married woman.

Soy soltera.
I'm a single woman.

Here, the marital status is presented as part of someone’s essential identity — how they are classified socially, not how they feel or what their current situation is.

⚠️ VIVO and MUERTO Always Expressed With ESTAR

Even though vivo and muerto might seem like “facts” about a person, Spanish treats them as biological states, not essential traits. Being alive or dead is understood as a condition, so Spanish uses ESTAR:

modules.title: SER & ESTAR With Adjectives

modules.html:
Other Equivalents of 'to be' in Spanish besides SER & ESTAR

HABER

HABER is an equivalent of to be used to express existence: there is / there are.
The most common forms are:
  • hay (present)
  • había (past, descriptive)
  • hubo (past, completed)

Hay muchas librerías en Buenos Aires.
There are a lot of bookstores in Buenos Aires.

Antes no había tantas casas por esta zona.
There used to not be so many houses in this area.

Anoche hubo mucha gente en el centro.
Last night there were a lot of people downtown.

HABÍA is used to describe a background state or setting.

HUBO refers to something that existed during a specific, completed timeframe.

HACER

HACER is used to talk about certain weather conditions that we would express in English with "to be".

TENER

TENER often translates as to have, but in many idiomatic expressions, it works like "to be" in English—especially when describing age, physical sensations, or mental states. 

These expressions reflect how the person feels or what they experience, and they rely on the body/mind as the conceptual container of that experience.
